explanations.answer: Now get her for me as a wife
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Samson comes home from Timnah and says, "I have seen a daughter of the Philistines in Timnah. Now get her for me as a wife." No warm-up, no small talk. He walks in the door and goes straight to the request.

explanations.answer: She has invited us all to Timnah
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions an invitation from her. Samson says he has seen a daughter of the Philistines in Timnah, then asks his parents to get her for him as a wife. That's the whole message.

explanations.answer: Her father wants to meet you both
explanations.explanation: Her father doesn't show up in this conversation at all. Samson only tells his parents what he saw and says, "Now get her for me as a wife." He doesn't mention anyone wanting to meet anyone. It's a short speech, baker, and it stays on one subject.

explanations.answer: Can't you find a wife among our own people
explanations.explanation: Right on the dough. His father and mother ask, "Can’t you find a young woman among your relatives or among any of our people? Must you go to the uncircumcised Philistines to get a wife?" They ask it as two questions, one right after the other. I think they were hoping he'd say yes to the first one.

explanations.answer: Why were you in Timnah without us
explanations.explanation: That question isn't in the text. What his parents ask is whether he can find a young woman among their relatives or their people. Their words are about where he finds a wife, not where he was walking around.

explanations.answer: Has her father agreed to any of this
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have his parents ask about her father. They ask whether Samson can't find a wife among his relatives or their people, and whether he must go to the Philistines. Her father isn't part of this talk yet.

explanations.answer: This was from the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The writer steps in with a side note: his father and mother "…did not know this was from the LORD, who was seeking an occasion to move against the Philistines…" So there's more going on than a young man and what he likes. The LORD is working in it, and Samson's parents can't see that yet.

explanations.answer: She was already promised to someone
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the passage says that. The side note is about the LORD, not about any promise she'd made. His parents didn't know this was from the LORD, who was seeking an occasion to move against the Philistines.

explanations.answer: Samson had met her family before
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that either. Samson's trip to Timnah is when he saw her, and the writer's side note points somewhere else. His parents didn't know this was from the LORD. That's the thing they were missing.

explanations.answer: ruling
explanations.explanation: That's it. The text says the LORD was seeking an occasion to move against the Philistines, "for at that time the Philistines were ruling over Israel." Israel had Philistines in charge of things. That's the situation the whole story sits in.

explanations.answer: mourning
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say the Philistines were mourning anything. It says they were ruling over Israel at that time. That's the situation, and the writer gives it plainly.

explanations.answer: rejoicing
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't describe the Philistines rejoicing. It says they were ruling over Israel at that time, and that's the reason the writer gives for the LORD seeking an occasion to move against them. One word makes the difference, baker.

explanations.answer: lion
explanations.explanation: A young lion, baker. Samson's walking through the vineyards of Timnah when it comes roaring at him. I'd have started a brand new career in sprinting, gold base and all. The text keeps it simple: a young lion, and it's roaring.

explanations.answer: bear
explanations.explanation: No bear in this story. The text says a young lion came roaring at Samson in the vineyards of Timnah. And the lion matters later, so keep it in your pocket.

explanations.answer: boar
explanations.explanation: A boar isn't in the passage. What comes roaring at Samson is a young lion, and a boar doesn't roar anyway. It happens right there in the vineyards of Timnah.

explanations.answer: Tears it apart with his bare hands
explanations.explanation: That's what happens. The Spirit of the LORD comes powerfully upon Samson, and he tears the lion apart with his bare hands, "…as one would tear a young goat." No weapon is mentioned at all. And this is the Spirit's doing, baker, not just a strong afternoon.

explanations.answer: Drives it off with his staff
explanations.explanation: The text never mentions a staff. It says the Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon Samson and he tore the lion apart with his bare hands. Nothing is driven off. The lion is done.

explanations.answer: Chases it out of the vineyards
explanations.explanation: No chasing in this one. The text says Samson tore the lion apart with his bare hands, as one would tear a young goat. The Spirit of the LORD came powerfully upon him first. By the end of it, the lion isn't going anywhere.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: It's the other way around. The text says Samson "…did not tell his father or mother what he had done." They were walking to Timnah with him, and he said nothing about the lion.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Judges 14:6 says he did not tell his father or mother what he had done. Samson tore a lion apart and then kept it to himself. Hold on to that, because this secret is going to matter.

explanations.answer: bees
explanations.explanation: Bees, baker. Samson leaves the road to see the lion's carcass, and in it is a swarm of bees. That's an unexpected tenant. The honey comes along with them.

explanations.answer: honey
explanations.explanation: Honey. The text says in the carcass was a swarm of bees, "…along with their honey." Samson scoops some into his hands and eats it as he goes. A lion and then honey, in the same story.

explanations.answer: birds
explanations.explanation: No birds in the text. Inside the lion's carcass is a swarm of bees, along with their honey. A small thing in a big story, but that's what Samson finds.

explanations.answer: grain
explanations.explanation: Grain isn't in the passage. What Samson finds in the lion's carcass is a swarm of bees, along with their honey. Honey is the thing he scoops up and eats along the way.

explanations.answer: locusts
explanations.explanation: Locusts don't show up here. In the carcass Samson finds a swarm of bees, along with their honey. It's still a swarm, but the right kind.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. When Samson returns to his father and mother, he gives them some honey and they eat it. He eats his handful on the way, then shares with them. The part he leaves out comes next.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: It's true, baker. The text says that when he returned to his father and mother, "…he gave some to them and they ate it." Samson shares the honey. He just doesn't share where it came from.

explanations.answer: He took it from the lion's carcass
explanations.explanation: That's what he leaves out. The text says he "…did not tell them that he had taken the honey from the lion’s carcass." His father and mother eat the honey he gives them, and he doesn't tell them where it came from. It's the second secret of the lion, baker.

explanations.answer: The woman in Timnah gave it to him
explanations.explanation: The woman doesn't give him any honey in the text. Samson took it from the lion's carcass himself, and he didn't tell his father and mother that. That's the part he left out.

explanations.answer: He traded for it at the market in Timnah
explanations.explanation: There's no market or trade in the passage. Samson scooped the honey out of the lion's carcass. When he gave some to his father and mother, he didn't tell them that.

explanations.answer: thirty
explanations.explanation: Thirty. When the Philistines saw Samson, they selected thirty men to accompany him. That's a big crowd, baker. And it matters for the bet that comes next.

explanations.answer: seven
explanations.explanation: Seven is the number of days of the feast, not the number of men. The text says the Philistines selected thirty men to accompany Samson. It's an easy one to mix up with the seven days.

explanations.answer: twelve
explanations.explanation: Twelve isn't the number in this passage. The Philistines selected thirty men to accompany Samson. That number comes back in the bet he makes.

explanations.answer: Thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes
explanations.explanation: That's the bet. Samson says, "If you can solve it for me within the seven days of the feast, I will give you thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes." Thirty men, thirty garments, thirty sets. And if they can't solve it, they owe him the same.

explanations.answer: Thirty shekels of silver and thirty young goats
explanations.explanation: Silver and goats aren't in this bet. Samson offers thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes if they solve the riddle within the seven days of the feast. His stake is clothes.

explanations.answer: Thirty donkeys and thirty bronze shields
explanations.explanation: Donkeys and shields don't show up. What Samson puts on the table is thirty linen garments and thirty sets of clothes. All of it is clothing.

explanations.answer: The honey in the lion's carcass
explanations.explanation: That's what the riddle is about. The eater is the lion and the strong one is the lion. The something sweet is the honey Samson found in the carcass (Judges 14:8-9). And he never told his father and mother where that honey came from (Judges 14:9).

explanations.answer: The grapes in the vineyards of Timnah
explanations.explanation: The vineyards are where the lion came roaring, but the riddle isn't about grapes. It's about what Samson found in the lion's carcass afterward: honey. The eater and the strong one is the lion, and the sweet thing is the honey.

explanations.answer: The feast he prepared for the wedding
explanations.explanation: The feast is where he tells the riddle, not what the riddle is about. The sweet thing that came out of the strong one is the honey from the lion's carcass (Judges 14:8-9). The feast is just where the riddle gets told.

explanations.answer: wife
explanations.explanation: His wife. On the fourth day the men say to her, "Entice your husband to explain the riddle to us, or we will burn you and your father’s household to death." That's a heavy thing to say to anyone. I think she was in a hard spot.

explanations.answer: father
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't send them to his father. They go to Samson's wife and tell her to entice her husband to explain the riddle. And what they say to her is serious.

explanations.answer: mother
explanations.explanation: His mother isn't part of this. The thirty men go to Samson's wife on the fourth day. It was his wife who got the threat.

explanations.answer: You do not really love me
explanations.explanation: That's what she says. Weeping, she tells him, "You hate me! You do not really love me! You have posed to my people a riddle, but have not explained it to me." The riddle was a bet with her people, and she wanted the answer. Samson doesn't give it to her yet.

explanations.answer: My father wants you to leave
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have her say that. She comes to him weeping and says he hates her and doesn't really love her. She also says he gave her people a riddle but hasn't explained it to her.

explanations.answer: The feast has to end tonight
explanations.explanation: No one says the feast has to end. She comes weeping and says, "You do not really love me!" She also says he has not explained the riddle to her. The feast keeps going for the whole seven days.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: It was much longer than that. The text says "She wept the whole seven days of the feast…" That's a week of it, baker. It wasn't one hard day.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: Right. Judges 14:17 says she wept the whole seven days of the feast. On the seventh day, because she had pressed him so much, he finally told her the answer. It was a long week.

explanations.answer: Explains the riddle to her people
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. After Samson tells her, the text says "…in turn she explained the riddle to her people." She had been weeping for seven days, so I think that answer didn't stay put for long. Then, before sunset on the seventh day, the men of the city say to Samson, "What is sweeter than honey? And what is stronger than a lion?"

explanations.answer: Keeps it to herself until the feast ends
explanations.explanation: She doesn't keep it. The text says that in turn she explained the riddle to her people. They come to Samson before sunset on the seventh day, so it's still the feast.

explanations.answer: Tells it to Samson's father and mother
explanations.explanation: His father and mother aren't who she tells. She explains the riddle to her people, the same ones she had been under pressure from. Samson had said he hadn't explained it to his parents, either.

explanations.answer: Gives them to the men who solved the riddle
explanations.explanation: That's what happens. The text says Samson "…gave their clothes to those who had solved the riddle." So the bet gets paid. Still, this one is a heavy part, because it comes after he killed thirty men at Ashkelon.

explanations.answer: Takes them home to his father's house
explanations.explanation: The clothes don't go home with him. He gives them to those who had solved the riddle. After that, he goes back to his father's house burning with anger.

explanations.answer: Leaves them with his wife's father
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say his wife's father gets the clothes. Samson gives them to the men who solved the riddle. That's where the bet ends.

explanations.answer: True
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. After the clothes are handed over, the text says "…burning with anger, Samson returned to his father’s house…" The riddle, the pressure and the bet all end in anger. And his father's house is where he heads.

explanations.answer: False
explanations.explanation: It's true, baker. The text says Samson went down to Ashkelon and gave the clothes to those who had solved the riddle. Then, "…burning with anger, Samson returned to his father’s house…" He pays the bet first, and then he goes home.

explanations.answer: She is given to one of the men who accompanied him
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says: "…his wife was given to one of the men who had accompanied him." I think this one hurts, baker. Samson went home, and the story doesn't stay quiet about what happened next.

explanations.answer: She goes with Samson to his father's house
explanations.explanation: The text says Samson returned to his father's house, but it doesn't say she went with him. Instead, his wife was given to one of the men who had accompanied him. It's a hard line, baker.

explanations.answer: She is sent away to live in Ashkelon
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say she goes to Ashkelon. Ashkelon is where Samson goes to get the clothes. What it does say is that his wife was given to one of the men who had accompanied him. That's all it says about her here.
